newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Rains ease off in Ivory Coast cocoa areas.
newsitem.headline: Rains ease off in Ivory Coast cocoa areas.

text.p: Light rains in southern Ivory Coast's cocoa belt eased off in early March after breaking a drought that had threatened to reduce mid-crop (April-Sept) harvests, analysts said on Tuesday.
Official data for the first 10 days of March showed rains at 10 weather stations totalled 169.4 mm against 122.4 in the previous 10 days and 282.7 mm for first 10 days of March 1996.
Crop analysts said cocoa trees showed little sign of being stressed.
"Trees have mechanisms to cope with seasons," said one.
Below average rains in the first 20 days of February had led to concern that trees would suffer, reducing mid-crop potential by killing flowers and developing pods and by reducing bean sizes.
"(Mid-crop) estimates will depend not only on the weather but how adjustments, if any, are made for carryover (of stock by speculators) to next year (1997/98)," said the analyst.
Pod counters have slated provisional mid-crop volumes between 80,000 and 180,000 tonnes, but final estimates had not been completed, industry and crop analysts said.

Two large cocoa buyers have pencilled in intial estimates of between 150,000 and 180,000 tonnes -- down on last year's unexpected 200,000 tonnes, which led to a record total crop of 1.2 million tonnes.
All said figures would be reviewed in April, when rains usually pick up and pods on trees give a better idea of yields.

Data from Ivory Coast's national weather station showed the following rainfall for the first 10 days of March in key growing areas plus the commercial capital Abidjan: Dalao 18.0 mm, Gagnoa 5.9 mm, San Pedro 4.0 mm, Tabou 0.5 mm, Man 65.5 mm, Dimbokro 11.3 mm, Yamoussoukro 15 mm, Abidjan 23.4 mm, Sassandra 0.5 mm, Adiake 27.8 mm, Korhogo 0.0 mm.
